text:
Another fantastic video. One thing I'll share after using my 6800xt for a few days is that you can solve the game clip recording issues (i.e. AMD Relive issues) by changing the "Video Encoding Type" option within the General Settings of the Radeon Software (just scroll down to the recordings section) from AVC (default) to HEVC. HEVC is a more modern codec which has better quality and half the size. I noticed zero performance hit when using this codec as the card supports this type of encoding in hardware. 

So why would AMD not enable this by default? Well, when you select HEVC, Windows 10 won't have it, so it asks you if you want to purchase the codec from the MS Store for $0.99 (99 cents USD). It's only a buck and totally worth it if you like recording HQ game clips. I'm sure there are other ways to implement the HEVC codec as well. You'll also probably want to bump up the recording resolution, fps, and bit rate in addition to the codec to capture really high quality video. It's all standard stuff that you'd do with Nvidia cards as well.

Regardless, once enabled, I get gameplay capture performance equal to that of the NVENC on my 2070 Super that I upgraded from and all is well. Best of all, no more corrupted videos, at least in my case.

the "are the additional features worth 50$?" debate, I already got it when I picked up my own GPU in May.

I found that the 100€ more asked for the 2070S were completely worth it when it comes to the additional features you'd get with the card in itself : NVenc Encoder both for your stream and capture, slightly better drivers, and better performance when it comes to productivity.

@-pcmr-108  It's not just for video. The dynamic range setting in the NVIDIA control panel affects the entire display at all times. You can literally see the desktop black level shift when you switch from the default Limited setting over HDMI to Full. 

The setting adjusts the RGB color range for the entire HDMI output. This means it affects everything coming out of the HDMI port at all times. The Limited setting sets the dynamic range to 16-235 RGB range while the full sets it to 0-255. Desktop monitors by default require 0-255 value, although you can change that in the settings. However, TVs are set to accept 16-235, which is why NVIDIA defaults to using the Limited preset over HDMI. The assumption that NVIDIA makes is that you will use the HDMI port only when connecting to a TV and DisplayPort when connecting to a monitor, which always outputs at the full 0-255 range and doesn't even have the dynamic range setting. 

So no, it doesn't just affect videos. Again, you can literally see your entire screen change when you change this setting. The video settings are separate and not what we are talking about here.
